question_addressed: Does sprouting/germination alter NOVA Group 1 minimal processing status, and do primary sources define sprouted grains/pulses?
findings: Primary NOVA literature (FAO 2019; Monteiro et al. 2016, 2018, 2019) is completely silent on sprouting and germination. Neither term appears in text, tables, or examples. Group 1 defines minimal processing as processes that "do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances to the original food" (FAO 2019, p. 11), enumerating physical and biological processes (drying, crushing, grinding, non-alcoholic fermentation, roasting, boiling), but omits sprouting. Under statutory standards (AACC International 2008; US FDA Whole Grain Guidance 2006; FSSAI Standards 2011), sprouted grains are defined as intact kernels that have undergone controlled germination while retaining original bran, germ, and endosperm.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "Unprocessed foods altered by industrial processes such as removal of inedible or unwanted parts, drying, powdering, squeezing, crushing, grinding, fractioning, steaming, poaching, boiling, roasting, and pasteurization, chilling, freezing, placing in containers, vacuum packaging, non-alcoholic fermentation, and other methods that do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances to the original food."; FDA Whole Grain Guidance (2006): "Malted or sprouted grains containing all of the original bran, germ, and endosperm shall be considered whole grains as long as sprout growth does not exceed kernel length and nutrient values have not diminished."
conflicts: none (all primary NOVA sources are uniformly silent)
absence: No primary NOVA document mentions sprouted, sprouting, or germination. Neither permitted nor excluded explicitly.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether biological germination falls under the general Group 1 clause ("other methods that do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances") or if silence requires continued abstention.

question_addressed: Does the declaration of "vitamins and minerals" indicate ultra-processing (Group 4) or remain compatible with Group 1/2/3 foods?
findings: FAO 2019 Table 1 explicitly places foods with added vitamins and minerals in Group 1 ("foods with vitamins and minerals added generally to replace nutrients lost during processing, such as wheat or corn flour fortified with iron and folic acid", p. 11) and Group 2 ("group 2 items with added vitamins or minerals, such as iodised salt", p. 11). Furthermore, vitamins and minerals are omitted from the list of Group 4 marker substances (no culinary use, p. 9) and cosmetic additives (p. 9-10). However, Monteiro et al. 2018 (Public Health Nutrition 21(1): 5-17) critique fortification in commercial ultra-processed foods as health-washing, noting that synthetic micronutrient addition to multi-ingredient products does not alter their Group 4 classification when formulated with Group 4 substances/additives.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "...and foods with vitamins and minerals added generally to replace nutrients lost during processing, such as wheat or corn flour fortified with iron and folic acid."; FAO 2019 p. 11: "...and group 2 items with added vitamins or minerals, such as iodised salt."; FAO 2019 p. 9: "Substances that are sources of energy and nutrients that are of no or rare culinary use such as high fructose corn syrup, hydrogenated or interesterified oils, and protein isolates..." [vitamins/minerals not listed].
sources_used: https://www.fao.org/3/ca5644en/ca5644en.pdf (FAO 2019, pp. 9, 11); https://doi.org/10.1017/S1368980018003762 (Monteiro et al. 2019); https://doi.org/10.1017/S1368980017000234 (Monteiro et al. 2018)
conflicts: NOVA Group 1/2 definitions explicitly permit added vitamins and minerals for nutrient replacement/public health, whereas epidemiological commentaries observe that standalone vitamin/mineral declarations predominantly appear on Group 4 formulated products.
absence: NOVA sources establish that vitamins and minerals do not make a food Group 4 on their own, but are silent on how to classify a standalone declaration "Vitamins and Minerals" on multi-ingredient composite foods when unaccompanied by individual chemical names.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether standalone "vitamins and minerals" is neutral/ignored (verdict determined by the food matrix) or triggers an abstention when appearing outside staple flour/salt.

question_addressed: Does "fortified" or "enriched" indicate industrial ultra-processing (Group 4) or standard staple processing (Group 1)?
findings: FAO 2019 explicitly gives fortified staple flour as an example of Group 1: "wheat or corn flour fortified with iron and folic acid" (p. 11). Statutory regulations (US 21 CFR §104.20, 21 CFR §137.165; FSSAI Fortification Regulations 2018) legally define "fortified" and "enriched" as the addition of specific micronutrients to conform to public health standards (e.g. enriched flour, fortified oil with vitamins A & D). NOVA primary literature treats fortification as non-exclusionary for Group 1 flours, but notes that fortification of snacks/cereals does not prevent them from being Group 4 if other markers are present.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "...such as wheat or corn flour fortified with iron and folic acid."; 21 CFR §104.20(a): "The Food and Drug Administration does not encourage pervasive promotions to fortify foods, but recognizes that dietary supplements and fortifying of foods with essential nutrients are appropriate in certain circumstances."; FSSAI Fortification Reg 2018: "'Fortification' means deliberately increasing the content of essential micronutrients in a food."
conflicts: none (explicitly Group 1 for staple flours; non-protective for formulated foods)
absence: NOVA does not define a blanket classification for the word "fortified" across non-staple foods.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "fortified" on staple bases (flour, rice, milk, oil) is treated as a Group 1/2 descriptor, or if fortification outside mandatory standards triggers scrutiny.

question_addressed: Is "premix" (e.g. vitamin premix, mineral premix) recognized by NOVA, and does it indicate an industrial formulation?
findings: The word "premix" is completely absent from FAO 2019 and all Monteiro et al. literature. In food manufacturing and statutory definitions (FSSAI Fortification Regulations 2018, Reg 2(1)(d)), a "premix" is defined as a uniform blend of micronutrients with an edible carrier used to facilitate dosing during food manufacturing.
quotes: FSSAI Fortification Regulations 2018, Reg 2(1)(d): "'Fortified food premix' means a blend of desired essential nutrients in combination with a carrier food substance."
conflicts: none (NOVA is silent)
absence: No primary NOVA document mentions "premix".
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "premix" is treated as synonymous with "vitamins and minerals" or as an industrial carrier mixture.

question_addressed: Does malting classify a grain as Group 1 (minimal processing) or Group 4 (industrial modification / maltodextrin precursor)?
findings: Primary NOVA sources do not explicitly place the verb/adjective "malted" in Group 1 examples, but FAO 2019 p. 9 lists "maltodextrin" as an ultra-processed marker sugar. In food science and 21 CFR §184.1445, "malt" is defined as sprouted and kiln-dried barley/grain containing active amylase enzymes. Whole malted grain (e.g. malted barley) is minimally processed, whereas malt extract and maltodextrin involve fractionation and enzymatic hydrolysis.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 9: "include varieties of sugars (fructose, high-fructose corn syrup, 'fruit juice concentrates', invert sugar, maltodextrin, dextrose, lactose)"; 21 CFR §184.1445: "Malt is an enzyme preparation obtained from barley which has been germinated under controlled conditions."
conflicts: Malted whole grains are sprouted grains (biological germination), but processed malt derivatives (malt extract, maltodextrin) are industrial ingredients.
absence: NOVA does not explicitly define the boundary between malted grain (flour) and malt syrup/extract.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "malted" grain/flour is treated as Group 1 or if "malted" requires specific distinction from malt extract.

question_addressed: When does an "extract" indicate a Group 4 marker substance versus a traditional culinary process?
findings: FAO 2019 presents a dual treatment for extraction. On p. 11, extraction is cited as the basic method for Group 2 culinary ingredients ("obtained directly from group 1 foods or from nature by processes such as pressing, refining, grinding, milling and drying"). However, on p. 9, industrial protein/flavor extracts ("meat, yeast and other extracts") are explicitly enumerated among ingredients characteristic of Group 4 ultra-processed foods. Furthermore, botanical extracts used as flavoring substances fall under cosmetic additives (p. 9-10).
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 9: "Substances that are sources of energy and nutrients that are of no or rare culinary use such as high fructose corn syrup... meat, yeast and other extracts..."; FAO 2019 p. 11: "Group 2... obtained directly from group 1 foods or from nature by processes such as pressing, refining, grinding, milling and drying."
conflicts: Extraction is both a Group 2 manufacturing technique (vegetable oil, sugar) and a Group 4 marker class ("meat, yeast and other extracts").
absence: NOVA does not provide an exhaustive rule for botanical/herbal/spice extracts (e.g. "rosemary extract", "tea extract", "celery extract") vs pure flavor extracts.
residual_gap: Senior review must establish clear boundary rules distinguishing Group 4 industrial flavor/protein extracts from Group 2 culinary concentrates and food extracts.

question_addressed: Are plain cereal flakes (e.g. rolled oats, corn flakes) classified as Group 1, 3, or 4 in NOVA?
findings: FAO 2019 explicitly includes plain cereal flakes in Group 1: Table 1 (p. 11) lists "flakes or rolled grains" under Group 1. Page 10 further clarifies: "plain corn flakes (Group 1), but with added sugar they are Group 3, and with flavouring or colour they are Group 4". Thus, flaking itself is an accepted physical minimal process; classification shifts to Group 3 or 4 only upon the addition of sugar, fats, or cosmetic additives.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 10: "...so plain corn flakes (Group 1), but with added sugar they are Group 3, and with flavouring or colour they are Group 4."; FAO 2019 p. 11 (Table 1): "cereals, grains such as... flakes or rolled grains".
conflicts: none (explicit text in FAO 2019 resolves the processing hierarchy: plain = Group 1; +sugar = Group 3; +flavor/color = Group 4)
absence: Commercial breakfast cereal products sold under "corn flakes" almost universally contain sugar, malt extract, and salt, creating confusion between generic "flaked maize" and branded products.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "flaked [grain]" in an ingredient list inherits Group 1 status as a physical form descriptor.

question_addressed: Does puffing or popping (e.g. puffed rice, popcorn) classify as Group 1 minimal processing?
findings: FAO 2019 does not explicitly use the words "puffed" or "popped" in Table 1, but Monteiro et al. 2019 explicitly list plain popcorn as Group 1 (unprocessed/minimally processed), while microwave popcorn with butter/salt is Group 3, and flavored/caramel popcorn is Group 4. Puffing is a thermal/pressure physical transformation without added substances.
quotes: Monteiro et al. 2019 (Public Health Nutrition 22(5): 936-941): "Plain popcorn kernels (group 1), freshly popped popcorn with butter and salt (group 3), pre-packaged microwave popcorn with artificial flavouring (group 4)."; FAO 2019 p. 11: "processes such as... roasting, and other methods that do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances".
conflicts: none (plain thermal expansion without additives is Group 1)
absence: FAO 2019 omits the specific terms "puffed" and "popped" from its primary physical process listing.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether to formally recognize "puffed" and "popped" as Group 1 physical descriptors in Foodscan descriptors.csv.

question_addressed: Is toasting recognized as an accepted Group 1 thermal minimal process?
findings: FAO 2019 Table 1 explicitly includes "roasting" in Group 1 ("steaming, poaching, boiling, roasting", p. 11). Toasting is physically identical to dry-heat surface roasting. In dictionaries and food culinary usage, toasting and roasting are synonymous thermal heating processes without chemical modification.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "steaming, poaching, boiling, roasting, and pasteurization... and other methods that do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances".
sources_used: https://www.fao.org/3/ca5644en/ca5644en.pdf (FAO 2019, p. 11); Merriam-Webster Unabridged ("toast: to brown or dry by heating")
conflicts: none (roasting is explicit in FAO 2019 Table 1)
absence: The word "toasted" specifically is not explicitly listed in FAO 2019 (only "roasting" is named).
residual_gap: Senior review can evaluate whether "toasted" should map to "roasted" or be added directly to descriptors.csv.

question_addressed: Does chemical or oxidative bleaching (e.g. bleached flour, bleached oil) make an ingredient ultra-processed (Group 4)?
findings: FAO 2019 does not list "bleaching" as a Group 4 marker. However, in industrial flour milling and oil refining, bleaching is a standard secondary refining step (using benzoyl peroxide, chlorine dioxide, or activated bleaching earth). In FAO 2019 Table 1 (p. 11), "refined" vegetable oils are placed in Group 2, and refined white flours are placed in Group 1. Bleaching of oils is an integral step in the production of Group 2 refined oils.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "Group 2... obtained directly from group 1 foods or from nature by processes such as pressing, refining, grinding, milling and drying."; 21 CFR §137.105: "Flour, white flour, wheat flour, plain flour... may be bleached with one or more of the optional bleaching agents..."
conflicts: none (bleaching is a standard industrial refining process; does not introduce Group 4 marker substances)
absence: NOVA texts do not mention bleaching of flours explicitly.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "bleached" is recognized as a descriptor or requires scrutiny on flours.

question_addressed: Is deodorisation an accepted step of Group 2 culinary ingredient refining?
findings: FAO 2019 Table 1 (p. 11) places "vegetable oils" obtained by "refining" in Group 2. In industrial edible oil processing (FSSAI Regulations 2011, Codex Alimentarius), refining consists of degumming, neutralizing, bleaching, and deodorising. Deodorisation is steam stripping under vacuum to remove volatile free fatty acids and odor compounds.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "Group 2... obtained directly from group 1 foods or from nature by processes such as pressing, refining, grinding, milling and drying."; FSSAI Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, Reg 2.2.1: "Refined vegetable oil means any vegetable oil which is obtained by... neutralisation, bleaching and deodorisation."
conflicts: none (sub-process of refining, which is explicitly Group 2 in FAO 2019)
absence: FAO 2019 lists "refining" collectively rather than detailing the unit operation "deodorisation".
residual_gap: Senior review can evaluate whether "deodorised" should be treated as a synonym/descriptor under Group 2 refined oil.

question_addressed: Does reconstitution (e.g. reconstituted milk, reconstituted juice) alter Group 1 status?
findings: FAO 2019 Table 1 (p. 11) notes that powdered milk and dried juices undergo industrial alteration, but pasteurized milk is Group 1. Under statutory rules (US FDA, FSSAI 2011), "reconstituted" means restoring dried/concentrated food to its original moisture content using potable water. FAO 2019 p. 9 lists "fruit juice concentrates" as an ingredient characteristic of Group 4 when used as a sugar replacer, but does not explicitly address reconstituted liquid milk.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 9: "include varieties of sugars (fructose, high-fructose corn syrup, ‘fruit juice concentrates’, invert sugar...)"; FSSAI 2011 Reg 2.1.1: "'Reconstituted milk or milk product' means a product which results from the addition of water to the dried or concentrated form of the product in the amount necessary to re-establish the appropriate water-to-solids ratio."
conflicts: Juice concentrate is a Group 4 marker when added to other foods, but reconstituted juice/milk consumed as such is ambiguously treated across NOVA studies.
absence: NOVA literature does not explicitly state whether reconstituting powdered milk with water yields Group 1, Group 3, or Group 4.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "reconstituted" ingredients trigger an abstention or inherit the status of their base food.

question_addressed: Does defatting (e.g. defatted soya flour) constitute fractionation yielding a Group 4 protein isolate or a Group 1 flour?
findings: FAO 2019 Table 1 lists "fractioning" among the industrial minimal processes for Group 1: "industrial processes such as removal of inedible or unwanted parts, drying, powdering, squeezing, crushing, grinding, fractioning..." (p. 11). However, p. 9 lists "protein isolates" (such as soya protein isolate) as characteristic Group 4 markers. In food processing standards, defatted soya flour is whole ground de-oiled soybean meal (containing ~50% protein, fiber, and carbohydrates), distinct from soya protein isolate (>90% protein, chemically precipitated).
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "industrial processes such as... crushing, grinding, fractioning, steaming..."; FAO 2019 p. 9: "sources of protein (hydrolysed proteins, soya protein isolate, gluten, casein, whey protein)"; 21 CFR §170.30: Defatted soy flour is recognized as distinct from soy protein concentrate and isolate.
conflicts: Fractioning is listed as a Group 1 process (p. 11), but industrial fractionation into purified fractions (protein isolates, modified oils) yields Group 4 markers (p. 9).
absence: NOVA does not explicitly define the exact threshold between defatted flour (Group 1 vs Group 4) and protein concentrate/isolate.
residual_gap: Senior review must clarify whether "defatted [grain/seed] flour" is accepted as a Group 1 fractioned flour or scrutinized as an industrial protein precursor.

question_addressed: Does "fractionated" oil or fat indicate Group 2 processing or Group 4 ultra-processing?
findings: FAO 2019 p. 11 includes "fractioning" in the general definition of processes applied to Group 1 foods. However, on p. 9, modified oils ("hydrogenated or interesterified oils") are listed as Group 4 markers. In fats and oils manufacturing, fractionation is dry or solvent crystallization separating liquid olein from solid stearin without chemical bonding changes.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "fractioning, steaming, poaching, boiling..."; FAO 2019 p. 9: "modified oils (hydrogenated or interesterified oils)".
conflicts: Fractioning is explicitly named as a process under Group 1, but fractionated fat fractions (e.g. fractionated palm kernel oil) are used almost exclusively as cocoa butter substitutes in Group 4 confectionery.
absence: NOVA does not explicitly place "fractionated oil" into Group 2 vs Group 4.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether fractionated vegetable fats constitute Group 2 culinary ingredients or Group 4 modified fats.

question_addressed: What does "compounded" mean on Indian labels (specifically "compounded asafoetida"), and how does NOVA treat it?
findings: FAO 2019 and Monteiro et al. have zero mentions of "compounded" or "asafoetida". In Indian statutory food standards (FSSAI Regulations 2011, Reg 2.9.2), "Compounded Asafoetida" (commonly Bandhani Hing) is an official legal designation for pure asafoetida gum blended with edible starches/flours (edible cereal flour like rice/wheat flour and gum arabic) to dilute the resin for culinary home use. Under NOVA principles, spices are Group 1 (FAO 2019 p. 11) and plain cereal flours are Group 1; blending two Group 1 foods without sugar/fat/cosmetic additives maintains Group 1 minimal processing.
quotes: FSSAI Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2011, Reg 2.9.2: "'Compounded asafoetida' or Bandhani Hing is composed of, one or more varieties of asafoetida (Irani or Pathani, or both) and gum arabic, edible starches or edible cereal flour."; FAO 2019 p. 11: "herbs, spices such as... garlic, oregano... mixtures of whole or broken spices".
conflicts: none (NOVA is silent; Indian statutory standard defines it as spice + flour/gum blend)
absence: NOVA literature never mentions compounded spices or asafoetida.
residual_gap: Senior review must decide whether "compounded asafoetida" is recognized as an Indian spice alias/blend or requires manual decomposition into its ingredients.

question_addressed: Does non-alcoholic fermentation alter Group 1 status, and what are its limits under NOVA?
findings: FAO 2019 explicitly lists "non-alcoholic fermentation" as an allowed minimal process in Group 1 (p. 11). Table 1 (p. 11) places plain fermented milk (yogurt, kefir, curd) in Group 1, provided no sugar, artificial sweeteners, flavors, or cosmetic additives are added. When sugar or fruits are added to fermented products (e.g. sweetened fruit yogurt), they become Group 3 or Group 4.
quotes: FAO 2019 (ca5644en.pdf) p. 11: "...vacuum packaging, non-alcoholic fermentation, and other methods that do not add salt, sugar, oils or fats or other food substances..."; FAO 2019 p. 11: "plain yoghurt, with no added sugar or artificial sweeteners".
conflicts: none (explicit in FAO 2019 Table 1 and definition)
absence: Traditional fermented Asian foods (tempeh, miso, idli batter) are not comprehensively enumerated in FAO 2019 Table 1.
residual_gap: Senior review can evaluate adding "fermented" as an explicit non-altering Group 1 descriptor for dairy and traditional foods.
